Agreed on next steps: update prompt deck, run 2k-sample regression, share security docs, schedule canary rollout.

transcript:
[00:00] Samir (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. We got about 45 minutes, we'll go over the latest quality eval, the one-off regression we saw on the clinical summarization set, and then next steps. Maya, Ethan, thanks for making time.
[00:18] Dr. Maya (Celestia): Yeah thanks Samir. Quick note, Priya had a conflict but she should be on shortly, might be joining in five.
[00:26] Jia (Redwood SE): Cool. I'll share screen in a sec — the results csv is in the drive link I posted in chat, link: drive.google.com/redwood/poc/celestia/results-2026-06-16.csv (note: internal link).
[00:40] Ethan (Celestia): Got it, I can see it. Quick high level, overall scores look similar but we noticed one of the scoring buckets dropped for the discharge summary prompts, is that the regression you mentioned?
[00:52] Jia: Yes, exactly. On the automated rubric the pass rate dropped from 88% to 81% for the discharge-summary prompt set after we applied the new temperature/penalty defaults last week. The human-in-the-loop checks also flagged a handful of hallucinations — 6 out of the 200 sampled.
[01:10] Dr. Maya: Hmm, 6/200 is... not catastrophic but given these are clinical notes we want near-zero hallucination. What changed in the pipeline?
[01:19] Jia: Two small changes: we lowered nucleus sampling threshold (top-p) from 0.95 to 0.9 to reduce token variance, and we applied a lighter repetition penalty. In most cases it reduced fluff, but for a few edge cases the model started inventing specifics when the prompt lacked anchored facts.
[01:36] Samir: To add, we also rolled a newer prompt template with a shorter system instruction to reduce token usage. That likely reduced context anchoring. So it's a compound effect: sampling + slightly weaker system prompt.
[01:49] Priya (joining): Sorry, joining now — Priya here. Can you recap quickly?
[01:53] Dr. Maya: We saw a dip in pass rate for discharge summaries after tweaks; a few hallucinations. Priya: Ok I saw the examples, thanks.
[02:04] Samir: Jia, could you walk through a couple of the flagged examples?
[02:08] Jia: Sure. Example one: patient record lacked antibiotic name, model filled in "cefazolin" — wrong. Example two: model fabricated a lab value of "Na 142" when the record only said 'electrolytes stable'. The scoring rubric marks hallucination when an assertion is unsupported by source. In our human review, these were marked as false positives.
[02:33] Ethan: The hallucination classifier is currently using embedding-sim semantic similarity with a threshold of 0.75; we saw those examples slip above threshold because the generated phrase used similar clinical phrasing.
[02:44] Jia: Right, embeddings can overestimate similarity for very common phrases. We recommended adding a binary fact-checker guardrail that rejects any asserted lab values or drug names unless present verbatim in the source or matched by structured field mapping.
[02:56] Dr. Maya: That sounds reasonable — could be a simple heuristic for now. We don't need perfect NLI, just a conservative reject-and-flag policy.
[03:05] Samir: Agreed. We can implement a rule: if output contains a numeric lab value or drug mention and there's no explicit match in source text or chart fields, then mark as 'requires review' and set score to fail (or low confidence). Jia: We can prototype that quickly.
[03:19] Priya: From compliance side, we also need to see audit logs for the runs and guarantee no PHI left in ephemeral logs. Ruben — can you confirm what Redwood stores?
[03:27] Ruben (CSM): Sure — for POC we store minimal metadata, and payload retention is configurable. I'll send the SOC2 + retained-logs one-pager; default hosted keeps logs for 7 days but we can change retention and enable customer-managed KMS on Dedicated/Private.
[03:40] Priya: Good. Is there a HIPAA-specific attachment?
[03:43] Ruben: We'll include HIPAA scoping doc — it's in the security folder, will share link.
[03:47] Ethan: Back to model tuning: Jia, what about adjusting decoding instead of top-p? Maybe lowering temperature from 0.8 to 0.6 and keep top-p at 0.95?
[03:58] Jia: We tried temperature tweaks in staging. Lowering temp helped reduce hallucinations but increased repetition in some long summaries. There's a tradeoff. Our recommendation is: 1) restore stronger system prompt (explicit instructions to only use provided facts), 2) set temperature to 0.6 and top-p back to 0.95, 3) add the fact-check guardrail, and 4) enforce a threshold on model confidence / embedding-sim for auto-accept.
[04:24] Dr. Maya: What about thresholds? Do you have numbers?
[04:27] Jia: From the 2k-sample runs we ran yesterday, embedding similarity >0.78 corresponds to 92% precision on our annotated set; but recall drops. For low-risk auto-accept we recommend 0.85; for borderline (0.78-0.85) we send to human review. It's conservative but reduces risk.
[04:43] Ethan: That matches what we saw. Human review capacity is limited though — we can handle roughly 150 reviews/week. So automated thresholds need to be tuned to keep review volume under that.
[04:53] Samir: Then can we run a projection? Jia: Yes, we can do a projected human review volume for a 10k/day run with the proposed thresholds; I'll include that in the 2k regression results.
[05:03] Priya: Also let's make sure the audit trail records the exact prompt used (including system message), model version, and any guardrail actions.
[05:11] Ruben: That is already in the plan — we log prompt hash, model id, request id, and guardrail decision. If you want full verbatim storage, we can enable but that's a retention decision.
[05:22] Dr. Maya: Ok good. Any other regressions?
[05:25] Jia: There was a small latency uptick when we enabled prefix caching on one of the dedicated instances — about 40ms median increase for the 2k sample — likely due to cache miss penalties while kv-cache warmed. We think that's temporary.
[05:37] Ethan: Latency is fine as long as p95 stays under 600ms, which it does; median at 230ms.
[05:43] Samir: Great. For rollout we propose a canary: 5% traffic with new prompts + guardrails on hosted, monitor hallucination rate and human review volume for 7 days, then increase to 25% if green. Jia will run the regression tests first.
[05:58] Dr. Maya: Sounds good. On the scoring rubric we had a question: can we make the 'critical-fail' category stricter for clinical assertions? Right now scoring 1-5, maybe add a 'Critical' flag that forces automatic escalation.
[06:10] Jia: Yes we can add a binary critical flag. In the spreadsheet we'll add a column 'critical_issue' and it'll map to immediate fail + page workflow.
[06:18] Samir: Cool. Any blockers on SOC2 or KMS? Priya: We need the HIPAA scoping doc, as mentioned, and confirmation of customer-managed KMS availability on dedicated. Ruben: Confirmed, customer-managed KMS is available on Dedicated and Private, I'll include config steps.
[06:33] Ethan: One more ask — can Redwood share the exact system prompt we used in the latest run so we can diff it against previous version?
[06:38] Jia: Yes, I'll paste both prompts into the shared prompt deck and highlight changes. Link: drive.google.com/redwood/poc/celestia/prompt-deck-2026-06-17.md
[06:48] Dr. Maya: Perfect. Timeline?
[06:50] Samir: We'll do immediate items: Samir shares prompt deck + spreadsheet by tomorrow (06-18), Jia runs 2k regression and posts results by 06-24, Ruben sends SOC2 + HIPAA scoping docs by 06-18, Priya to confirm compliance Qs by 06-21, and we aim for canary the week of 06-29.
[07:07] Priya: That timeline works for compliance.
[07:10] Ethan: I'll assemble the 3 edge-case transcripts and drop them in the shared folder by 06-20.
[07:16] Samir: Great. Anything else?
[07:19] Dr. Maya: One tiny nit — can we get a quick workshop with SEs to go over prompt authoring best practices for clinical contexts? Maybe 60 minutes.
[07:27] Samir: Yes — Jia and I can do a session next week. We'll propose times in chat.
[07:33] Jia: Ok I'll set up a calendar invite.
[07:36] Samir: Thanks everyone. We'll follow up in email with links and action items.
[07:41] Dr. Maya: Thanks. End.
